newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia sees red faces at start of corruption talks.
newsitem.headline: Russia sees red faces at start of corruption talks.

text.p: Boris Nemtsov, Russia's new first deputy prime minister on Saturday grilled red-faced officials on the way they award government contracts in the latest round of the Kremlin's fight against corruption announced this week.

Boris Nemtsov even questioned the way the government contracted for massive repairs on its own White House headquarters, which was badly damaged after the Kremlin used tanks on it to quash an armed uprising in 1993.
"I don't understand why the main building in the country was repaired without a competition. I don't understand," Nemtsov said.

Government officials responded that an open tender for the contract had not been held because the government had been "in a hurry". Thousands of Turkish workers rapidly repaired the building in an estimated $85 million job.

Nemtsov's meeting on Saturday followed a decree and a speech by President Boris Yeltsin this week in which he vowed to stamp out the corruption that has flourished across Russia since the fall of communism in 1991.
Yeltsin said his latest attempt to grapple with the age-old problem would open up the system of tendering for state contracts to reduce the temptation faced by bureaucrats for illicit enrichment.
"I will bring this struggle to an end. It will become scary to steal and take bribes," the president said.

Chairing a special meeting at the White House called to examine how government ministries awarded state contracts, Nemtsov brushed aside bureaucrats' excuses for their failure to conduct open tenders.
"Procurements will no longer be carried out through this ordering system," he told officials who were unable to say how many of their supplies were obtained through open competition.
"Unfortunately, it's not uncommon that competitions are formally carried out but in fact they often already know who's going to win. That won't do," Nemtsov said.
Senior officials from the defence, transport and construction ministries said a lack of budget funding and monopoly suppliers contributed to the existing system of sweetheart deals.
But Nemtsov, a young liberal recently appointed to the government to help jumpstart stalled political and economic reform, did not appear sympathetic.
He said the Voyentorg Defense Ministery chain of stores sold goods at prices 50 percent higher than at ordinary shops, and would be among the organisations targeted for reform.
"We are also going to deal with Voyentorg, and very severely at that," Nemtsov warned, aiming a broadside at "people sitting here" who had tried to block previous efforts to reform the organisation.
Nemtsov said open tender competitions for state contracts, as well as tender results and any violations, would have to be published in the national and regional press.
Russia's deputy public prosecutor Vladimir Davydov told the meeting that 5,500 cases of bribery were registered in 1996.
There has been little evidence of success in Yeltsin's previous anti-corruption campaigns and few high-level criminal convictions.
